messages.content: Is this a good customer interview question? "Would you switch from your current bank for better rates?"
Not quite. Hypothetical switching is easy to say and hard to do. Try: "Have you ever switched banks? What made you do it, and what was the hardest part?"
Why do people say yes in interviews when they mean no?
Because they're kind, and because saying yes to a hypothetical costs nothing. Ask about what they did, and watch for commitments rather than compliments.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Are you the kind of person who plans meals?"
Not quite. Asks them to describe themselves rather than what they did. Try: "What did you have for dinner on Tuesday, and when did you decide on it?"
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Do you want to save time on grocery shopping?"
"Tell me about your last grocery trip, from deciding to go to putting things away." Everyone says yes to saving time.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Do you want to save time on grocery shopping?"
Not quite. Everyone says yes to saving time. Try: "Tell me about your last grocery trip, from deciding to go to putting things away."
Can I interview someone over text or email?
You can, but you'll lose the follow-ups and the tone. A short call or a meeting usually tells you far more.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Do you ever forget to water your plants?"
Not quite. A yes tells you little. Get the story. Try: "Tell me about the last plant you lost. What happened?"
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Do you like our new design?"
"Here's the screen: show me how you'd find last month's invoice." It invites a polite yes. Watch what they do with it instead.
What does it mean when someone says 'that's a great idea'?
Very little. Compliments are free. Ask what they'd stop doing, or would give up, to use it: their time, money, or attention.
Give me four opening questions for interviews about commuting by bike in the city.

1. Tell me about your ride this morning, from leaving home to locking up.
2. What went wrong on a ride recently, if anything?
3. What do you carry, and how do you carry it?
4. What made you start biking instead of another way?
Ask about real past events, and follow each answer with 'why?' or 'what happened next?'.
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Would you switch from your current bank for better rates?"
"Have you ever switched banks? What made you do it, and what was the hardest part?" Hypothetical switching is easy to say and hard to do.
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Do you ever forget to water your plants?"
"Tell me about the last plant you lost. What happened?" A yes tells you little. Get the story.
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "What features would you want?"
"What were you trying to get done the last time this tool let you down?" People are poor designers of features they haven't needed. Ask about the work.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Would a faster checkout make you shop here more?"
Not quite. Hypothetical, and it bundles a solution into the question. Try: "Tell me about the last time you gave up on buying something online. What happened?"
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Would an AI assistant help you write emails?"
"Show me the last email that took you a long time to write. What made it hard?" Puts a solution in their mouth.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Don't you hate filling out forms?"
Not quite. Leading and emotional. Ask about a real form. Try: "What's the last form you filled out? How long did it take, and what was annoying, if anything?"
Should I record interviews?
Only with permission, and say how you'll use and store it. Notes during the interview, written up right after, are often enough.
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "How often do you think you'd use this?"
"How many times last week did you do this task? Can you walk me through one?" A guess about the future.
Who should I interview first?

People who have the problem now and are already trying to solve it, even badly. Someone using a spreadsheet, a workaround or a competitor will teach you more than someone who agrees it sounds annoying.
How do I know if a problem is real?
Look for what people already spend on it: time, money, workarounds, complaints. If they've never tried to fix it, it probably isn't painful enough for them to change.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Wouldn't it be great if your bus told you exactly when it was coming?"
Not quite. Leading, and it sells the idea. Try: "How do you decide when to leave the house to catch the bus?"
Is this a good customer interview question? "Would you recommend this to your friends?"
Not quite. Asks for a promise about the future. Try: "Have you told anyone about a tool like this before? What did you say?"
How do I talk to people without making them feel sold to?
Mean it when you say you're learning. Ask about them, listen more than you talk, and don't bring slides. If you have nothing to sell yet, that's an advantage.
What is a 'job to be done'?

The progress someone is trying to make in a situation, like 'get dinner on the table on a weeknight', rather than the product they use to do it. People hire products for jobs and fire them when something does the job better.
Is this a good customer interview question? "How often do you think you'd use this?"
Not quite. A guess about the future. Try: "How many times last week did you do this task? Can you walk me through one?"
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Is our price too high?"
"What else did you look at before you came to us, and how did you compare them?" Asks for a judgment they have no reason to think about.
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Would you use an app that reminds you to drink water?"
"When did you last notice you hadn't drunk enough water? What did you do about it?" It asks about a future that hasn't happened, and people are kind about ideas. Ask about what they already do.
What if the person keeps talking about my idea?
Gently bring it back: 'Before we get to that, I'd love to hear about the last time you…' Their past is the part only they can tell you.
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Would you recommend this to your friends?"
"Have you told anyone about a tool like this before? What did you say?" Asks for a promise about the future.
How do I find people to interview?
Go where the people with the problem already are: the places, forums, shops and events tied to it. Ask each person you interview who else you should talk to.
How long should an interview be?
Twenty to forty minutes is usually enough. Plan for five or six open questions; you won't get through more if you follow up well.
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Don't you think scheduling meetings is frustrating?"
"Walk me through how the last meeting you set up got scheduled." It tells them the answer you want. Leave the feeling for them to name.
Is this a good customer interview question? "How much would you pay for this?"
Not quite. Prices people name for something they haven't used are guesses. Find what they already spend. Try: "What do you use for this today, and what does it cost you, in money or time?"
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Don't you hate filling out forms?"
"What's the last form you filled out? How long did it take, and what was annoying, if anything?" Leading and emotional. Ask about a real form.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Would you use an app that reminds you to drink water?"

Not quite. It asks about a future that hasn't happened, and people are kind about ideas. Ask about what they already do. Try: "When did you last notice you hadn't drunk enough water? What did you do about it?"
What should I write down?
Their words, not your summary of them. Note what they did, what it cost them, what they've tried, and any strong feeling. Mark which notes are facts and which are your guesses.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Is finding a babysitter a big problem for you?"
Not quite. Yes-or-no, and it plants the word 'problem'. Try: "How did you find someone the last time you needed childcare?"
Give me four opening questions for interviews about parents choosing after-school activities.

1. How did your child end up in the activity they do now?
2. Tell me about one you tried that didn't work out.
3. Who else was involved in deciding?
4. What does the week look like on the busiest day?
Ask about real past events, and follow each answer with 'why?' or 'what happened next?'.
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Would you use a map of accessible entrances?"
"Tell me about the last time you couldn't find a way into a building you needed to get into." Hypothetical. Ask about the last time it mattered.
What's a good follow-up question?
'Why?' and 'What happened next?' Or repeat their last few words back as a question. Most of the useful detail comes after the first answer.
What's the most common mistake in customer interviews?
Pitching. As soon as you describe your idea, people start being polite about it. Keep the conversation on their life and their past behavior, not your solution.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Is our price too high?"
Not quite. Asks for a judgment they have no reason to think about. Try: "What else did you look at before you came to us, and how did you compare them?"
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Do you agree that most students struggle with budgeting?"
"How did you keep track of money last month? What did you use?" Asks them to agree with your belief about others.
What is a good first question?
'Tell me about the last time you…' followed by the situation you're studying. It gets a story with real details instead of an opinion.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Don't you think scheduling meetings is frustrating?"
Not quite. It tells them the answer you want. Leave the feeling for them to name. Try: "Walk me through how the last meeting you set up got scheduled."
What is customer discovery?
Talking with the people you hope to help, before you build much, to learn how they deal with a problem today and whether it matters enough to them to change what they do.
How many people should I interview?
Keep going until you stop hearing new things: often between ten and twenty for one kind of person. If every interview surprises you, you're not done, or you're talking to too many kinds of people.
Is a survey the same as an interview?
No. Surveys count things you already know to ask about. Interviews find the things you didn't know to ask. Interview first, survey later if you need numbers.
How do I avoid leading questions?
Remove your opinion and your solution from the question. Ask how, what, when and 'tell me about', not 'don't you think' or 'would you'.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Would an AI assistant help you write emails?"
Not quite. Puts a solution in their mouth. Try: "Show me the last email that took you a long time to write. What made it hard?"
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "How much would you pay for this?"
"What do you use for this today, and what does it cost you, in money or time?" Prices people name for something they haven't used are guesses. Find what they already spend.
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Would a faster checkout make you shop here more?"
"Tell me about the last time you gave up on buying something online. What happened?" Hypothetical, and it bundles a solution into the question.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Would you use a map of accessible entrances?"
Not quite. Hypothetical. Ask about the last time it mattered. Try: "Tell me about the last time you couldn't find a way into a building you needed to get into."
Give me four opening questions for interviews about musicians booking gigs.

1. Tell me about the last gig you booked. How did it start?
2. What did you have to send, and to whom?
3. What happened with a booking that fell through?
4. How do you decide what to charge?
Ask about real past events, and follow each answer with 'why?' or 'what happened next?'.
Is this a good customer interview question? "What features would you want?"
Not quite. People are poor designers of features they haven't needed. Ask about the work. Try: "What were you trying to get done the last time this tool let you down?"
What should I ask about money?
Ask what they spend now: on tools, services, workarounds or time. Past spending is real; 'how much would you pay' is a guess.
How can interviews mislead me?
If you only talk to friends, ask hypotheticals, or hear what you hoped to, you'll leave confident and wrong. Talk to strangers, ask about the past, and write down what disproves your idea.
Give me four opening questions for interviews about small shops selling online.

1. Walk me through the last order you shipped.
2. What do you do when something goes wrong with an order?
3. What have you tried to get more people to your shop?
4. Which part of the week takes longest?
Ask about real past events, and follow each answer with 'why?' or 'what happened next?'.
Rewrite this interview question so it isn't leading: "Are you the kind of person who plans meals?"
"What did you have for dinner on Tuesday, and when did you decide on it?" Asks them to describe themselves rather than what they did.
Is this a good customer interview question? "Do you agree that most students struggle with budgeting?"
Not quite. Asks them to agree with your belief about others. Try: "How did you keep track of money last month? What did you use?"
How do I interview someone about something embarrassing?
Make it normal first: 'Lots of people tell me…' Ask about a specific time, let silence do some work, and never push when someone wants to stop.
Give me four opening questions for interviews about people caring for an older relative.

1. Tell me about the last time you helped them with an appointment.
2. Who else shares the care, and how do you keep each other informed?
3. What's something that went wrong recently?
4. What have you tried that made it easier?
Ask about real past events, and follow each answer with 'why?' or 'what happened next?'.
What do I do with all my interview notes?
Read them side by side and look for repeated stories, workarounds and words people use. Write down what surprised you, and what you now believe that you didn't before.
Give me four opening questions for interviews about students cooking on a budget.

1. What did you eat yesterday, and where did it come from?
2. Walk me through the last time you cooked for yourself.
3. What do you do when you run out of money before the end of the month?
4. Where do you get ideas for what to make?
Ask about real past events, and follow each answer with 'why?' or 'what happened next?'.
What's a 'commitment' in customer discovery?
Something the person gives up to move forward: time for another meeting, an introduction to a colleague, a pre-order, a pilot. Commitments tell you more than enthusiasm.
